spec.world: Key projects in Lisbon, Évora, and Porto. Principal Architect Joana de Vasconcelos and team. Real buildings: The Marvila Library Annex (€2,450,000, completed 2023), the Évora Municipal Archive (€3,100,000, in construction, set for Nov 2025), and the Alcantara Riverfront Steps. Architect-in-Charge

Joana de Vasconcelos

With Norte Sul Team

Commission

Lisbon Municipal Council

Public Competition (1st Place)

A physical anchor for collective memory in East Lisbon.

The Marvila Library Annex stands as a monument to slow time. Situated on a former industrial plot on Lisbon's eastern riverfront axis, the library extension addresses the historical fragmentation of the neighborhood by establishing a highly porous, civic threshold. Built almost entirely of locally sourced Lioz limestone and monolithic in-situ cast concrete, the building responds directly to the intense Atlantic light, diffusing sharp Southern shadows through monumental vertical louvers.

Inside, the structure prioritizes acoustic silence and sensory weight. Heavy, thick walls of raw concrete block out city noise, while large scale structural spans of Douglas fir timber and Portuguese cork ceiling tiles naturally regulate humidity and reverberation. It is a civic space designed to withstand both heavy public usage and the elements for generations to come.

"Norte Sul did not build us a temporary pavilion. They carved out a public hall of granite and light that feels as though it has always belonged to the soil of Marvila."

— Marvila Local Library Council Report, 2024

Spatial Specification

Material Authenticity

The transition from interior to public square is mediated by a series of monumental steps, structured using massive blocks of Portuguese Lioz stone. Over time, physical contact will polish the raw surface, registering the passage of citizens through the space.

  • check Lioz Limestone, Honed & Bush-hammered
  • check Cast-in-situ concrete (30% volcanic ash)
  • check High-density cork acoustic panelling

The Seasonality of Atlantic Light

Unlike northern public architecture, Portuguese civic design must contend with extreme light contrast. The deep recessed apertures on the southern elevation allow low winter sun to penetrate deep into the reading halls, while completely blocking the direct, harsh summer sun at high noon—drastically reducing the building's active HVAC footprint.

Philosophy

Civic spaces shaped by Atlantic light and Portuguese granite.

We view public buildings as direct civic responsibilities. In our work, we prioritize local materials—such as raw balsa timber, massive Lioz limestone, and high-density cork boards—ensuring that structures are physically rooted in the Portuguese landscape while enduring for centuries.

By aligning our layout strictness with classical Portuguese masonry, we design schools, municipal archives, and public libraries that serve as continuous communal stages, absorbing the high-contrast Atlantic sun.
